section.heading: 6.3. Volumes by Cylindrical Shells
section.paragraph: Some volume problems are very difficult to handle by the methods of the preceding section. For instance, let’s consider the problem of finding the volume of the solid obtained by rotating about the $$y$$ -axis the region bounded by $$y = 2x^{2} - x^{3}$$ and $$y = 0$$ . (See Figure 1.) If we slice perpendicular to the $$y$$ -axis, we get a washer. But to compute the inner radius and the outer radius of the washer, we’d have to solve the cubic equation $$y = 2x^{2} - x^{3}$$ for $$x$$ in terms of $$y$$ ; that’s not easy.

section.heading: The Method of Cylindrical Shells
section.paragraph: There is a method, called the method of cylindrical shells, that is easier to use in a case like the one shown in Figure 1. Figure 2 shows a cylindrical shell with inner radius $$r_{1}$$ , outer radius $$r_{2}$$ , and height $$h$$ . Its volume $$V$$ is calculated by subtracting the volume $$V_{1}$$ of the inner cylinder from the volume $$V_{2}$$ of the outer cylinder:

$$\begin{array}{l} {V = {V_{2} - V_{1}}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\pi r_{2}^{2}h - \pi r_{1}^{2}h = \pi\left( {r_{2}^{2} - r_{1}^{2}} \right)h}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {\pi\left( {r_{2} + r_{1}} \right)\left( {r_{2} - r_{1}} \right)h}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {2\pi\frac{r_{2} + r_{1}}{2}h\left( {r_{2} - r_{1}} \right)}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A three-dimensional rendering of a cylindrical shell of height h. The distance between the inner and outer walls is labeled Delta r. The inner radius is labeled r_1, the outer radius is labeled r_2, and the average radius of the shell is labeled r.

section.paragraph: If we let $$\Delta r = r_{2} - r_{1}$$ (the thickness of the shell) and $$r = \frac{1}{2}{\left( {r_{2} + r_{1}} \right)}$$ (the average radius of the shell), then this formula for the volume of a cylindrical shell becomes
$$V = 2\pi rh\Delta r$$
and it can be remembered as
$$V = \lbrack{circumference}\rbrack\lbrack{height}\rbrack\lbrack{thickness}\rbrack$$

Now let $$S$$ be the solid obtained by rotating about the $$y$$ -axis the region bounded by $$y = f(x)$$ [where $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ ], $$y = 0$$ , $$x = a$$ , and $$x = b$$ , where $$b > a \geqslant 0$$ . (See Figure 3.)

image.alt: Details The figure has two parts. The first part is a curve, three line segments, and a shaded region graphed on the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. There are two tick marks, a and b, on the x axis. The curve, y = f(x), begins at the top left, directly above a, goes down to the right, initially concave down, and then concave up. From a and b, two vertical line segments rise upward to meet the endpoints of the curve. A horizontal line segment connects a and b. The region bound by the curve and the three line segments is shaded. A curved arrow centered on the y axis points counterclockwise. The second part is a solid that resembles a bell-shaped solid mounted on a disk with a vertical cylindrical space at its center. The entire solid is centered on the y axis. The side of the bell traces the curve y = f(x). The inner and outer radii of the solid are a and b, respectively.

section.paragraph: We divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ of equal width $$\Delta x$$ and let $${\overline{x}}_{i}$$ be the midpoint of the $$i$$ th subinterval. If the rectangle with base $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ and height $$f\left( {\overline{x}}_{i} \right)$$ is rotated about the $$y$$ -axis, then the result is a cylindrical shell with average radius $${\overline{x}}_{i}$$ , height $$f\left( {\overline{x}}_{i} \right)$$ , and thickness $$\Delta x$$ . (See Figure 4). So by Formula 1 its volume is
$$V_{i} = \left( {2\pi{\overline{x}}_{i}} \right)\left\lbrack {f\left( {\overline{x}}_{i} \right)} \right\rbrack\Delta x$$

image.alt: Details The figure has three parts. In the first part, a curve, a solid, and a rectangle are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve labeled y = f(x), begins from directly above a on the x axis, briefly goes up to the right, concave down, and then goes down to the right, initially concave down and then becomes concave up, and then very briefly rises up to the right and ends directly above the mark b on the x axis. From the ends of the curve, perpendiculars are dropped to the x axis, meeting the axis at a and b. A cylindrical shell centered on the y axis rests with the center of its base on the origin. The cylinder is positioned such that the curve touches the midpoint of a vertical cross-sectional slice on the extreme right of the solid. From the midpoint of the top surface, a vertical dashed line segment reaches the x axis to meet it at x bar_i. The inner and outer surfaces of the slice lie on the marks x_(i minus 1) and x_i, respectively. In the second part of the figure, the same curve is present in this image. A series of 4 cylindrical shells of equal widths and centered on the y axis are wrapped over one another with the highest cylinder inner surface beginning at a and the outer surface of the shortest one positioned at b. The curve y = f(x) traces the midpoints of the top surfaces of the washers. From the inner and outer surfaces of the washers, perpendiculars are dropped to the x axis dividing the interval a and b into equal parts. In the third part of the figure, many thin cylindrical shells are overlapped. The right edges of their top surfaces lie on the curve f(x).

section.paragraph: Therefore an approximation to the volume $$V$$ of $$S$$ is given by the sum of the volumes of these shells:
$$V \approx {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{V_{i} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{2\pi{\overline{x}}_{i}f{\left( {\overline{x}}_{i} \right)}\Delta x}}}}$$
This approximation appears to become better as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . But, from the definition of an integral, we know that
$$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{2\pi{\overline{x}}_{i}f{\left( {\overline{x}}_{i} \right)}\Delta x = {\int_{a}^{b}{2\pi xf{(x)}dx}}}}$$
Thus the following formula appears plausible:
The volume of the solid in Figure 3, obtained by rotating about the $$y$$ -axis the region under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$a$$ to $$b$$ , is
$$V = {\int_{a}^{b}{2\pi xf(x)dx {where}0 \leqslant a < b}}$$
The argument using cylindrical shells makes Formula 2 seem reasonable, but later we will be able to prove it (see Exercise 7.1.81).

The best way to remember Formula 2 is to think of a typical shell, cut and flattened as in Figure 5, with radius $$x$$ , circumference $$2\pi x$$ , height $$f(x)$$ , and thickness $$\Delta x$$ or $$dx$$ :
$${V = \int_{a}^{b}}\underset{circumference}{\underset{︸}{\left( {2\pi x} \right)}}{\underset{height}{\underset{︸}{\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack}}}{\underset{thickness}{\underset{︸}{dx}}}$$

image.alt: Details The figure has two parts. The first part is a three-dimensional rendering of a cylindrical shell with its base centered at the origin. The midpoint of the width of the shell is at a distance x from the y axis. Its height is f(x). A vertical cross-section of the shell at its rightmost point is shaded. The second part is a three-dimensional rendering of a rectangular box of length 2 pi r, width Delta x, and height f(x).

section.paragraph: This type of reasoning will be helpful in other situations, such as when we rotate regions about lines other than the $$y$$ -axis.

section.paragraph: NOTE Comparing the solution of Example 1 with the remarks at the beginning of this section, we see that the method of cylindrical shells is much easier than the washer method for this problem. We did not have to find the coordinates of the local maximum and we did not have to solve the equation of the curve for $$x$$ in terms of $$y$$ . However, in other examples the methods of the preceding section may be easier.

section.heading: Disks and Washers versus Cylindrical Shells
section.paragraph: When computing the volume of a solid of revolution, how do we know whether to use disks (or washers) or cylindrical shells? There are several considerations to take into account: Is the region more easily described by top and bottom boundary curves of the form $$y = f(x)$$ , or by left and right boundaries $$x = g(y)$$ ? Which choice is easier to work with? Are the limits of integration easier to find for one variable versus the other? Does the region require two separate integrals when using $$x$$ as the variable but only one integral in $$y$$ ? Are we able to evaluate the integral we set up with our choice of variable?

If we decide that one variable is easier to work with than the other, then this dictates which method to use. Draw a sample rectangle in the region, corresponding to a cross-section of the solid. The thickness of the rectangle, either $$\Delta x$$ or $$\Delta y$$ , corresponds to the integration variable. If you imagine the rectangle revolving, it becomes either a disk (washer) or a shell. Sometimes either method works, as in the next example.

list.item: To find the volume using $$x$$ as the variable of integration, we draw the sample rectangle vertically, as in Figure 12(b). Rotating the region about the line $$x = - 1$$ produces cylindrical shells, so the volume is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = \int_{0}^{2}2\pi(x + 1)(2x - x^{2})\mathit{dx} = 2\pi\int_{0}^{2}(x^{2} + 2x - x^{3})\mathit{dx}} \\ {\phantom{V} = {2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{3}}{3} + x^{2} - \frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = \frac{16\pi}{3}}} \end{array}$$

To find the volume using y as the variable of integration, we draw the sample rectangle horizontally as in Figure 12(c). Rotating the region about the line produces washer-shaped cross-sections, so the volume is $$\begin{array}{l} {V = \int_{0}^{4}\left\lbrack \pi\left( \sqrt{y} + 1 \right)^{2} - \pi\left( \frac{1}{2}y + 1 \right)^{2} \right\rbrack\mathit{dy} = \pi\int_{0}^{4}\left( 2\sqrt{y} - \frac{1}{4}y^{2} \right)\mathit{dy}} \\ {\phantom{V} = \pi\left\lbrack \frac{4}{3}y^{3/2} - \frac{1}{12}y^{3} \right\rbrack_{0}^{4} = \frac{16\pi}{3}} \end{array}$$
